# KMP Platform Boundaries

Shared code is the default. Platform code exists only where an API is genuinely
platform-specific, and it stays small, named and replaceable.

## Where Code Goes

| Code | Location |
|---|---|
| Domain, ViewModels, mapping, UI, resources | `src/commonMain` of the owning module |
| Android-only APIs (Context, Activity results, CameraX, SpeechRecognizer, Keystore) | `src/androidMain` of the same module |
| iOS-only APIs (UIKit, AVFoundation, Speech, Keychain, Network, posix) | `src/iosMain` of the same module |
| App entry, notifications service, manifest | `:app` (Android only) |
| Navigation, app shell, ViewModel bindings, iOS entry | `:shared` (`MainViewController()` in `iosMain`) |
| Xcode project, Info.plist, Swift host, WidgetKit extension | `iosApp/` |

- `commonMain` never imports `java.*`, `android.*`, `androidx.activity`,
  `androidx.core`, OkHttp, or Okio. CI compiles iOS klibs on Linux and fails on
  leaks: `./gradlew compileKotlinIosSimulatorArm64`.
- Platform files use the `.android.kt` / `.ios.kt` suffix and the same package as
  the `expect` declaration.

## Choosing The Mechanism

- **Interface + Koin binding** for services with state, lifecycle, permissions or
  test fakes: `ServerStore`, `NetworkMonitor`, `AppVisibility`, `ServerDiscovery`
  are interfaces in `commonMain`, bound in `platformDataModule`
  (`core/data/src/{android,ios}Main/.../di/PlatformDataModule.kt`).
- **`expect fun` / `expect val`** for small stateless helpers: number/date
  formatting, logging, IDN conversion, `notificationsSupported`.
- **`expect` composables** for UI that needs a platform view or launcher: QR camera
  preview, attachment picker, dictation, back handling. Keep the shared screen
  and its state in common code; the `actual` only adapts the platform API.
- Avoid `expect class`; when a stateful platform object is needed, prefer an
  interface with platform implementations. Existing `expect object
  CacheDatabaseConstructor` is generated by Room and is the exception.
- Do not fake a platform feature: hide it (`notificationsSupported = false` on iOS)
  and document the gap.

## Common Replacements

| Instead of | Use in commonMain |
|---|---|
| `System.currentTimeMillis()` | `kotlin.time.Clock.System.now().toEpochMilliseconds()` |
| `java.time.*` | `kotlinx-datetime` (`TimeZone`, `LocalDate`); localized text via `expect` |
| `UUID.randomUUID()` | `kotlin.uuid.Uuid.random()` (opt-in) |
| `ConcurrentHashMap`, `synchronized` | `ConcurrentMap` in core:data, atomicfu `SynchronizedObject`, `Mutex` in suspend code |
| `android.util.Base64` | `kotlin.io.encoding.Base64` (padding optional when decoding untrusted data) |
| `String.format` | explicit formatting helpers (`formatDecimal`, `formatInteger`) |
| `BuildConfig` in libraries | values passed from the app (`AppInfo`), `Platform.isDebugBinary` on iOS |
| `@Volatile`, `@JvmInline` | `kotlin.concurrent.Volatile`, `kotlin.jvm.JvmInline` (explicit import) |

## Rules

- Keep Android behavior identical when moving code: the same storage files and
  keys, the same Room database, the same resources and semantics. A migration
  must not change what an upgrading user sees.
- Engines and platform callbacks may run on other threads or coroutines: emit
  from them with `channelFlow { send() }` or `callbackFlow`, never `flow { emit() }`.
- Objective-C exceptions abort the process and cannot be caught in Kotlin; check
  preconditions before calling APIs that raise them (e.g. an empty audio input
  format before `installTapOnBus`).
- New platform features need both actuals or an explicit, documented iOS gap.

## Verification

- `./gradlew :<module>:compileAndroidMain :<module>:compileKotlinIosSimulatorArm64`.
- Runtime changes: `android-runtime-verification` for Android and `kmp-ios` for iOS.

description: >
  Diagnoses and fixes slow Kotlin/Native compilation and linking in Kotlin
  Multiplatform projects that target iOS. Use when the user reports slow iOS or
  shared-framework builds, long linkDebug*/linkRelease* or XCFramework tasks,
  cold CI builds that re-download the Kotlin/Native toolchain, KSP or other
  generated code on the native path, transitiveExport usage, or asks for a
  local-development versus CI build performance plan.

# Kotlin/Native Build Performance

Turn "the iOS build is slow" into a measured diagnosis and a small set of safe
fixes. Two rules apply throughout:

1. Never trade away required release behavior. A faster local loop must not
   change what CI publishes.
2. Measure before and after with the same command and the same build state.
   An unmeasured fix is a guess.

## Step 0: Classify the Slow Scenario

Establish four facts before editing anything: **where** (local or CI),
**what** (debug feedback loop or release/distribution artifact), **state**
(first build, clean, warm, or no-op), and **phase** (which tasks dominate the
log). Then match the dominant symptom:

| Symptom in the build log | Likely cause | Read |
|---|---|---|
| `linkRelease*` or `*ReleaseXCFramework` tasks in a local development loop | Building distribution artifacts for development | [artifacts-and-targets](references/artifacts-and-targets.md) |
| Kotlin/Native compiler distribution downloaded on every CI run | `~/.konan` not preserved between runs | [caching-and-gradle](references/caching-and-gradle.md) |
| Long pause before the first task starts | Configuration phase, no configuration cache | [caching-and-gradle](references/caching-and-gradle.md) |
| All iOS targets build when only one simulator is needed | Broad task (`build`, `assemble`, `assemble*XCFramework`) or unused targets | [artifacts-and-targets](references/artifacts-and-targets.md) |
| `ksp*` tasks ahead of `compileKotlinIos*` | Generated-code work on the native path | [exports-and-generated-code](references/exports-and-generated-code.md) |
| Small source edit recompiles and relinks everything | Compiler caches disabled, or missing incrementality | [caching-and-gradle](references/caching-and-gradle.md), [experimental](references/experimental.md) |
| Machine overloaded while several `link*` tasks run at once | Parallel native linking | [caching-and-gradle](references/caching-and-gradle.md), worker-limit caveat |

## Step 1: Audit and Measure

1. Run the static audit from the project root:

   ```bash
   scripts/audit-native-build.sh /path/to/project
   ```

   It is read-only and prints `file:line` findings (disabled caches, broad
   local tasks, `transitiveExport`, broad KSP configuration, missing CI
   `.konan` cache), each pointing at the reference file with the fix.
   Findings are leads, not verdicts — confirm each against project policy.
2. Find the command the user actually waits for: a script, a CI step, or the
   Gradle invocation inside an Xcode build phase. Optimize that command, not
   a task you picked yourself.
3. Run it twice when practical. The first build downloads Kotlin/Native
   components and fills caches; only the second and later runs are
   representative. Attribute time per task before blaming the compiler:

   ```properties
   kotlin.build.report.output=file   # writes build/reports/kotlin-build/
   ```

   Gradle's `--scan` or `--profile` work too.
4. If you cannot run the build (no macOS host, no Xcode), analyze logs, build
   scans, or checked-in metrics instead — and state explicitly that the
   conclusion is static.

## Step 2: Fix in Safe Order

Apply fixes one at a time, re-measuring as you go:

1. **Restore healthy defaults** — remove cache/daemon workarounds, enable
   Gradle build and configuration caches, keep `~/.konan` warm in CI, update
   Kotlin: [references/caching-and-gradle.md](references/caching-and-gradle.md)
2. **Build only what the feedback loop needs** — one specific task per loop,
   correct integration method, justified target matrix:
   [references/artifacts-and-targets.md](references/artifacts-and-targets.md)
3. **Cut export and generated-code cost** — drop `transitiveExport`, narrow
   `export(...)`, scope KSP work to the native compilations that need it:
   [references/exports-and-generated-code.md](references/exports-and-generated-code.md)
4. **Experimental switches last, with the user's agreement**:
   [references/experimental.md](references/experimental.md)

## Worked Example

A developer on an Apple Silicon Mac complains that "every shared-module
change costs 12 minutes". Their loop runs `./gradlew :shared:assembleXCFramework`.
A build scan of the second (warm) run shows:

```
:shared:linkReleaseFrameworkIosArm64             348s
:shared:linkReleaseFrameworkIosX64               341s
:shared:compileKotlinIosX64                       96s
:shared:linkDebugFrameworkIosSimulatorArm64       41s
:shared:compileKotlinIosSimulatorArm64            38s
configuration phase                               64s
```

Reasoning chain:

- The loop is **local + debug + warm**, but ~690s goes to `linkRelease*` —
  release linking is an order of magnitude slower than debug and only CI
  needs it. Replace the local command with
  `:shared:linkDebugFrameworkIosSimulatorArm64` (or the Xcode embed task if
  Xcode drives the build). *(artifacts-and-targets)*
- All `iosX64` work serves Intel simulators; ask whether the team still
  supports them before removing the target. *(artifacts-and-targets)*
- 64s of configuration on every run disappears behind
  `org.gradle.configuration-cache=true` once trialed. *(caching-and-gradle)*
- Expected loop after the change: ~40s compile + ~40s link on warm builds —
  confirm by re-running the new command twice and comparing.
- CI keeps `assembleXCFramework` untouched; note that explicitly in the
  report.

## Verify

- [ ] Re-run the exact baseline command; compare warm build against warm
      build, not warm against cold.
- [ ] Second run with the configuration cache reports it is being reused.
- [ ] The local development log no longer contains `linkRelease*`,
      `*ReleaseXCFramework`, or removed generator tasks.
- [ ] CI still produces every required release artifact, unchanged.
- [ ] Tests pass and the app still runs from Xcode.
- [ ] `scripts/audit-native-build.sh` reports no findings you have not
      consciously accepted and documented.

## Report Your Changes

Close with a short performance note:

- The slow scenario (local/CI, debug/release, cold/warm) and the measured
  evidence — or a statement that the analysis was static.
- Each change, and why it is safe for release behavior.
- The before/after commands the user can run to confirm the win.
- Remaining tradeoffs: experimental flags enabled, targets removed under a
  policy assumption, worker limits, or generated-code work deferred.
- Links to the relevant official documentation below.

## Official Documentation

| Topic | Link |
|---|---|
| Improving Kotlin/Native compilation time | https://kotlinlang.org/docs/native-improving-compilation-time.html |
| Kotlin Gradle plugin compilation and caches | https://kotlinlang.org/docs/gradle-compilation-and-caches.html |
| iOS integration methods | https://kotlinlang.org/docs/multiplatform-ios-integration-overview.html |
| Direct integration with Xcode | https://kotlinlang.org/docs/multiplatform/multiplatform-direct-integration.html |
| Building final native binaries and XCFrameworks | https://kotlinlang.org/docs/multiplatform/multiplatform-build-native-binaries.html |
| Kotlin/Native binary options | https://kotlinlang.org/docs/native-binary-options.html |
| KSP with Kotlin Multiplatform | https://kotlinlang.org/docs/ksp-multiplatform.html |

# Maestro Android E2E

Use Maestro for complete user journeys, not as a substitute for unit or Compose
behavior tests. Read `.maestro/AGENTS.md`, the affected UI testTags, and one
comparable flow before editing.

## Selectors

- Interact through stable Compose `testTag` values exposed as resource IDs.
- Use visible text for assertions only when text content is the behavior under
  test.
- Do not use localized or dynamic text as an interaction selector.
- Do not use coordinates unless there is no semantic/tagged target and the
  limitation is documented.
- When a required interactive control has no testTag, add the tag in the app
  rather than weakening the flow.

## Credentials And State

- Never hardcode server passwords or pairing codes in YAML, scripts, docs,
  screenshots, logs, or responses.
- Connect flows receive a fresh pairing code via a CLI parameter, e.g.
  `-e OC_PAIR_CODE="$(opencode api post /api/pair --data '{}' | jq -r .code)"`,
  and reference `${OC_PAIR_CODE}`; codes are single-use and short-lived.
- Reuse an installed app with a saved server when the journey does not test
  connecting.
- Clear app state only when isolation requires it; it removes saved servers.
- Never capture a screenshot while a password or code field is populated.
- Do not send prompts in real sessions; prompting flows create a session in a
  disposable scratch directory.

## Flow Design

- One flow covers one coherent user journey.
- Extract repeated setup into a small `runFlow` subflow only when it retains
  clear failure assertions.
- Use `appId: io.github.beppe2880.opencodemobile.debug` for debug builds.
- Prefer deterministic setup and cleanup. Existing shared test data may persist,
  so create unique entities or remove only entities created by the flow.
- Use `extendedWaitUntil` for a named observable state after network/async work.
- Never use arbitrary sleeps.
- Hide the keyboard or press back before tapping covered controls.
- Replace existing field content before typing when append behavior is possible.
- Capture screenshots or hierarchy only at useful checkpoints/failure evidence.

## Assertions

Assert user-observable outcomes: destination, changed value, success feedback,
refreshed list, or durable state after relaunch. Avoid implementation-detail
assertions that belong in unit/Compose tests.

## Execution

Use the emulator serial reported by ADB or repository scripts; never hardcode a
serial-to-AVD mapping. Run the smallest relevant flow and keep output under the
gitignored `.maestro/output/` directory.

After failures, inspect the hierarchy, screenshots, server health
(`opencode api get /api/info`), and Logcat
before increasing timeouts.

name: product-ux-orchestrator
description: Entry skill for planning, optimizing, or reviewing user flows across the opencode-mobile Android app; asks how the user wants personas handled, routes to the smallest UX specialist set, and tracks plan versus implementation and runtime evidence.
---

# Product UX Orchestrator

Use this as the router for product-flow work. It owns scope, ordering, approval
gates, and completion status. It does not replace the specialist skills or the
subsystem implementation skills.

## Intake

Resolve these from the request and code before asking questions:

- feature and user goal;
- entry point and success state;
- phone, foldable/tablet, or both;
- task frequency and stakes;
- whether the user supplied a target flow or persona.

Ask only for information that changes the outcome. Batch ordinary scope gaps
into one concise question.

## User Perspective Gate

Never run a multi-persona simulation implicitly. If the request has not already
selected a perspective, ask exactly one question:

> How should I handle the user perspective: follow your decided direction,
> evaluate one target user, simulate multiple users, stay neutral and report
> observable friction only, or choose the smallest useful approach for you?

Interpret the answer as one of:

- `user-defined`: preserve the requested direction; identify blockers and
  tradeoffs without reopening product choices unnecessarily.
- `single-persona`: load `ux-user-panel` for one named or inferred persona.
- `multi-persona`: load `ux-user-panel` only after this explicit approval.
- `neutral`: do not predict preferences; report evidence and alternatives.
- `agent-selected`: choose the smallest useful mode and state why.

Do not ask when the prompt already answers the gate. Record the selected mode in
the plan so later verification uses the same criterion.

## Specialist Routing

- Load `ux-runtime-observer` to inspect an existing flow or verify a built flow.
- Load `ux-flow-audit` to diagnose interaction cost, feedback, recovery, state
  coverage, and unnecessary steps.
- Load `ux-user-panel` only for an approved single- or multi-persona prediction.
- Load `ux-information-architecture` only for findability, navigation, labels,
  grouping, hierarchy, or first-click questions.
- Load `ui-quality-review` after the flow is stable when rendered visual quality
  is in scope.
- Load `ux-implementation-review` during delivery and before completion.

For implementation, also load the owning project skills: `kmp-master` and its
specialists for `android/`. The OpenCode server is external; flows that need a
server change are out of scope and must be reported as constraints.

## Workflow For A New Flow

1. Resolve intake and the User Perspective Gate.
2. Inspect comparable product behavior and technical constraints.
3. Define current assumptions, non-goals, entry, success, cancellation, and
   recovery.
4. Run the approved user perspective analysis, if any.
5. Load the conditional IA review only when its trigger is present.
6. Produce current or baseline, safe, recommended, and power-user alternatives
   when those alternatives are meaningful.
7. Run `ux-flow-audit` on the proposed flow.
8. Stop for approval when the user is shaping the flow; do not hide a product
   decision inside implementation.
9. Create an implementation contract and hand off to subsystem skills.
10. Run implementation, runtime, and visual verification in that order.

## Workflow For An Existing Flow

1. Resolve intake and the User Perspective Gate.
2. Use `ux-runtime-observer` to exercise the current flow before judging it.
3. Use `ux-flow-audit` to produce evidence-backed findings.
4. Run only the approved persona analysis.
5. Compare alternatives and obtain approval before structural edits.
6. Implement through owning subsystem skills.
7. Re-run the same runtime scenario.
8. Use `ux-implementation-review` to compare plan, code, and observed result.

## Persistent Plan

For substantial work, write `plan-<feature>-ux.md` at the repository root when
the user asks for a plan, implementation begins, or a stable handoff is needed.
Use `references/plan-template.md`. Do not create a document for a quick verbal
review. Update the existing plan rather than creating competing reports.

## Completion Rule

`Complete` requires planned behavior implemented and runtime verified on every
in-scope platform. Compilation alone is `Statically verified`, not complete.
Report missing, blocked, intentionally divergent, and unverified items without
changing the plan to make delivery appear finished.

Read `references/evidence-and-metrics.md` whenever producing scores, preference
claims, before/after comparisons, or a completion verdict.

See `references/sources.md` for the external methods adapted into this project
and the constraints deliberately rejected.

name: ui-quality-review
description: Post-flow visual and interaction-quality review for rendered opencode-mobile Android UI; checks hierarchy, typography, spacing, states, accessibility, responsiveness, platform fit, and design-system consistency without changing approved product behavior for taste.

# UI Quality Review

Review rendered quality after the flow is defined or when the user explicitly
requests a visual audit. Product behavior belongs to `ux-flow-audit`; this skill
must not reopen approved flow decisions merely to create a more fashionable UI.

## Evidence First

Use screenshots and the actual runtime when possible. Code can prove tokens,
semantics, and state branches, but not final rendering. Load
`android-runtime-verification`. Review phone and, when relevant, foldable or
tablet widths, in light and dark theme.

## Review Dimensions

- attention order and primary-action hierarchy;
- grouping, alignment, whitespace, density, and content scan path;
- typography scale, line length, weight, and truncation;
- semantic color roles, contrast, dark mode, and non-color cues;
- component consistency, radius, border, elevation, and token drift;
- default, hover/press, focus, selected, disabled, loading, empty, error, and
  success states;
- keyboard, screen-reader semantics, touch targets, reduced motion, font scale,
  RTL, and insets as relevant;
- responsive reflow rather than squeezed desktop layouts;
- visual trust, authentic content, and avoidance of generic card-heavy or
  decorative UI that obscures the task.

Preserve the established `Oc*` Compose design system, which follows the OpenCode
V2 visual language (`docs/design-system.md`), unless the user explicitly
requests a redesign.

## Finding Schema

```text
ID: UI-<number>
Severity: Blocker | High | Medium | Low
Confidence:
Rendered location:
Observation:
User consequence:
Recommendation:
System/token impact:
```

Taste disagreements cannot be Blocker or High. Accessibility, unreadable
content, hidden actions, broken responsive layouts, and missing task states can.

## Output

Lead with prioritized findings, then list strengths to preserve, responsive and
state coverage, design-system drift, and unverified scenarios. Do not claim a
visual fix until the changed runtime is rendered and reviewed again.

name: ux-flow-audit
description: Evidence-based audit of an existing or proposed opencode-mobile task flow; diagnoses interaction cost, cognitive load, forms, feedback, state coverage, errors, recovery, and unnecessary steps without assuming fewer clicks are always better.
---

# UX Flow Audit

Audit one defined task from entry to success. Existing flows require runtime
evidence from `ux-runtime-observer` when feasible. Proposed flows may be audited
as designs, with runtime claims clearly unavailable.

## Scope Gate

Confirm goal, entry, success, platform, audience mode, frequency, stakes, and
available evidence. Do not silently widen a flow review into a product-wide
audit. Audit before editing when the request asks for both review and fixes.

## Evaluation Spine

For every step assess:

- information scent and clarity of the next action;
- number and ambiguity of decisions;
- recognition versus recall;
- whether data can be prefilled, remembered, inferred, or removed;
- whether a separate screen or confirmation is justified;
- feedback, progress, success, and perceived waiting;
- error prevention, preservation of input, recovery, cancel, back, and undo;
- loading, empty, sparse, error, offline/interruption, and overflow states as
  relevant;
- first-time discoverability and repeat-use efficiency;
- consistency with platform and existing product conventions;
- accessibility as ability to complete the task, not a late checklist;
- trust and intentional friction for sensitive or irreversible actions.

Use Krug and Nielsen as diagnostic prompts, not as reasons by themselves. Every
finding must name the user consequence. Do not penalize expert density, required
regulatory input, or safety steps merely because they increase counts.

## Step Challenge

Ask of every step:

1. Must it exist?
2. Does the system already know the information?
3. Can it remain inline or in the current context?
4. Can a sensible default or a remembered choice remove work?
5. Can a single-choice state auto-select safely?
6. Is confirmation proportional to consequence?
7. Would recent items, favorites, autocomplete, bulk action, deep link, or a
   shortcut improve repeat use?
8. Does removing the step increase ambiguity, error risk, or cognitive load?

## Alternatives

When optimization is requested, produce only meaningful alternatives:

- current or baseline flow;
- safe optimization with minimal structural change;
- recommended flow balancing clarity and efficiency;
- power-user path when the task is frequent enough to justify one.

Compare alternatives with the shared Interaction Cost rubric. Show counted
events; do not present a bare score or fabricated completion-time percentage.

## Finding Schema

```text
ID: FLOW-<number>
Severity: Blocker | High | Medium | Low
Confidence:
Location/step:
Evidence:
User consequence:
Recommendation:
Tradeoff:
Effort: S | M | L
```

Blocker means the core task cannot be completed or risks irreversible loss.
High means significant failure or hesitation on the core path. Medium costs
time or quality but remains recoverable. Low is real polish, not taste disguised
as severity.

## Output

Provide scope/evidence, current flow map, metrics, highest-impact findings,
alternatives, recommended flow, preserved strengths, open hypotheses, and what
needs analytics or user research. For substantial implementation work, update
the existing `plan-<feature>-ux.md` rather than creating a competing report.

Read `.opencode/skills/product-ux-orchestrator/references/evidence-and-metrics.md`.

description: Compares an approved Product UX plan with opencode-mobile code, tests and Android runtime evidence; tracks each requirement as implemented, statically verified, runtime verified, divergent, missing, or blocked before declaring completion.

# UX Implementation Review

Use during delivery and before completion. This skill audits conformance to the
approved flow and state contract; it does not rewrite the plan to match whatever
was built.

## Inputs

- the approved `plan-<feature>-ux.md` or explicit conversation plan;
- affected Android code;
- generated contracts where relevant;
- test and build results;
- runtime evidence from `ux-runtime-observer` and platform verification skills.

If no stable plan exists, reconstruct only explicit requirements and label the
rest `No approved baseline`; do not fabricate intended behavior.

## Requirement States

- `Not started`
- `Implemented`
- `Statically verified`
- `Runtime verified`
- `UX verified`
- `Diverged intentionally`
- `Missing`
- `Blocked`

`Complete` requires runtime evidence for every in-scope behavior whose outcome
is user-visible. Build success never upgrades an item beyond `Statically
verified`.

## Review

1. Expand the plan into atomic, testable requirements.
2. Trace each requirement to owning code and platform.
3. Check entry, happy path, loading, empty, validation, error, recovery,
   cancellation/back, success feedback, interruption, and power-user behavior
   that the plan includes.
4. Verify phone/wide-layout parity only where the plan requires it.
5. Match tests and runtime evidence to requirements, not merely files changed.
6. Record unplanned additions and whether they alter the approved flow.
7. Re-run the same baseline scenario after fixes so before/after metrics remain
   comparable.

## Output

Use a matrix:

| Requirement | Code | Static evidence | Runtime evidence | Status | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

Then report planned count, implemented count, runtime-verified count, missing,
blocked, intentional divergence, and an overall verdict:

- `Complete`
- `Partial`
- `Blocked`
- `No approved baseline`

Update the existing plan checklist when one exists. Preserve failed or missing
items; never mark them complete based on intent.

# UX Information Architecture

Use this skill when the product question is where a capability belongs, what it
should be called, or how users navigate to it. Do not load it for an isolated
form or visual-polish task.

## Inputs

- target audience mode and goal;
- current route and navigation structure;
- product concepts and existing labels;
- frequency and importance of the destination;
- technical constraints that affect stable URLs or cross-platform exposure.

## Analysis

1. State the user's likely task-oriented mental model without inventing
   demographic detail.
2. Inventory current primary, secondary, utility, contextual, search, and direct
   entry paths.
3. Run a predicted first-click walkthrough for only the approved persona mode.
4. Apply the trunk test: identity, current location, major sections, available
   actions, hierarchy, and search must be recoverable from the screen.
5. Compare audience language with internal implementation terminology.
6. Check grouping overlap, catch-all categories, depth, route consistency,
   breadcrumbs where hierarchy is deep, and whether search is masking poor IA.
7. Preserve direct URLs and platform conventions when proposing changes.

## Honesty Rules

A predicted first click is not a real first-click test. A simulated grouping is
not card sorting. Label these as `Predicted preference` or `Hypothesis`; state
when tree testing, analytics, search logs, or real user research is required.

Do not impose generic limits such as seven navigation items without naming the
actual scanning or findability consequence in this product.

## Output

Provide current IA, target mental model, predicted first click, label findings,
recommended placement, alternative entry points, route/navigation implementation
notes, and validation gaps. A common valid result is one canonical management
location plus a contextual quick action, not moving the entire feature.

Use the shared evidence labels from
`.opencode/skills/product-ux-orchestrator/references/evidence-and-metrics.md`.

# UX Runtime Observer

Gather runtime evidence before UX judgment. This skill observes and measures; it
does not redesign the flow or claim user preferences.

## Platform Routing

- Android: read `android/AGENTS.md`, load `kmp-master` and
  `android-runtime-verification`, use an emulator connected to the local OpenCode
  server, and use
  Mobile MCP or Maestro.
- The official OpenCode web UI on the server port is a reference for comparison,
  not a target to measure.

Reuse the tools and credential workflow already documented by the project.

## Observation Contract

Define before starting:

- persona mode selected by the orchestrator;
- exact goal, entry point, and success state;
- starting account/data state;
- platform and viewport/device;
- states and metrics to capture;
- destructive actions that require safe test data or must not be executed.

## Per-Step Record

```text
Step:
Screen/state:
User intent:
Available choices:
Action:
Expected response:
Actual response:
Feedback:
Wait:
Backtracking:
Result:
Evidence:
```

Count screens, actions, decisions, manual inputs, context switches, waits,
scroll, backtracking, recovery, and time to value. Time only a repeatable run;
otherwise mark it estimated or unavailable. Use screenshots for material visual
states, not every pointer movement.

## Required Checks

- Navigate from the real entry point rather than opening only the destination
  unless direct-entry behavior is the thing under test.
- Exercise the happy path and one representative error or recovery path when
  safe and relevant.
- Inspect crashes and Logcat on Android.
- Check phone and wide layouts when layout can change.
- Record unavailable states instead of inventing them.

## Output

Return a neutral flow map, metric table, evidence paths, code-versus-runtime
discrepancies, and unobserved states. Do not assign preference or visual taste.
Hand the evidence to `ux-flow-audit`, `ux-user-panel`, or `ui-quality-review` as
appropriate.

Use `.opencode/skills/product-ux-orchestrator/references/evidence-and-metrics.md`
for labels and metric definitions.

# UX User Panel

This skill predicts how defined user perspectives may interpret and prefer a
flow. It does not observe real human behavior.

## Activation Gate

Do not load or run a multi-persona panel unless the user explicitly selected it
or told `product-ux-orchestrator` to choose the approach. If the user already
specified the desired flow, preserve that direction and use a panel only when
asked to challenge or compare it.

For a single-persona request, evaluate only that persona. Do not add a standard
panel for completeness.

## Default Personas

- `first-time`: unfamiliar with product structure and terminology; values clear
  labels, visible next actions, and confidence.
- `returning`: knows the product broadly but not every location; values
  continuity, remembered choices, recent items, and predictable placement.
- `power-user`: repeats the task frequently; values shortcuts, bulk actions,
  keyboard paths, deep links, and minimal repetition.
- `cautious`: prioritizes consequences, reversibility, privacy, and recovery;
  accepts intentional friction when stakes justify it.

Replace these with domain-specific personas when the user supplies them. Do not
invent demographic attributes that do not change task behavior.

## Walkthrough Protocol

For each persona and each material step, answer before interaction:

1. What am I trying to achieve now?
2. Where would I look first?
3. What would I choose and why?
4. What do I expect to happen?
5. What makes me hesitate or requires interpretation?

After interaction or review of the proposed response:

1. Did the result match the expectation?
2. Is the next action clear?
3. Is feedback sufficient?
4. Would I prefer to remain in context or change screen?
5. Would repetition make this step annoying?
6. Which alternative would I prefer, and what tradeoff drives that choice?

Every claimed feeling must trace to an event, label, missing response, or
decision. Remove generic emotional narration.

## Comparison Output

For each persona provide:

```text
Persona:
Likely first action:
Preferred flow:
Reason:
Rejected alternative:
Main tension:
Evidence basis:
Claim type: Predicted preference
Confidence: High | Medium | Low
```

Then synthesize:

- agreement across perspectives;
- meaningful disagreements;
- recommended default;
- optional accelerator or safer path;
- what needs analytics or real user research to settle.

Never average conflicting personas into one vague "user". A valid result can be
a simple default for newcomers plus an accelerator for frequent users.

Use the evidence labels from
`.opencode/skills/product-ux-orchestrator/references/evidence-and-metrics.md`.

# Contributing

Thanks for helping! This guide covers how to build the app, the conventions the code follows
and what a pull request needs. Automated checks enforce the title and template rules:
issues and pull requests that still miss them after 72 hours are closed.

## Before you start

- **Bugs and features**: open an issue from a template first, so we can agree on the approach
  before you write code. Small fixes and typos can go straight to a pull request.
- **AI tools are welcome**, but you must understand and test what you submit. Long
  AI-generated descriptions get closed.
- Never put server addresses, passwords, pairing codes or private sessions in issues,
  screenshots, logs or test fixtures.

## Build and run

Requirements: JDK 21, the Android SDK (compile SDK 37), and an OpenCode 2.x server.

```bash
cd android
./gradlew :app:installDebug          # debug build: io.github.beppe2880.opencodemobile.debug, "OpenCode Mobile Dev"
./gradlew :app:installDebug -PfakeData=true   # sample data, no server needed
```

On an emulator the host's server is at `http://10.0.2.2:4096` and shows up under "Found on
this network"; alternatively `adb reverse tcp:4096 tcp:4096` makes it reachable at
`http://localhost:4096`. Pair with `opencode pair`.

The iOS app (`iosApp/`) needs macOS with Xcode: open `iosApp/iosApp.xcodeproj` and run it on
a simulator, or build it from the command line as described in
[`android/AGENTS.md`](android/AGENTS.md#ios). Most code is shared in `android/`, so iOS
compile errors also show up on Linux with `./gradlew compileKotlinIosSimulatorArm64`.

Before opening a pull request, run what CI runs:

```bash
(cd android && ./gradlew spotlessCheck testDebugUnitTest :app:lintDebug :app:assembleDebug compileKotlinIosSimulatorArm64)
(cd tools/api-gen && bun install && bun run check)   # only if you touched the API or the generator
```

For terminal WebView changes, also run `bun test tools/terminal-touch.test.ts` from the root.
After changing the Android widget strings (`widget_*` in `android/app/src/main/res`), run
`bun tools/ios-widget-strings.ts` to update the iOS widget's String Catalog.

## Code conventions

The architecture and rules are documented in [`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md) and
[`android/AGENTS.md`](android/AGENTS.md) (they also guide AI coding agents). In short:

- **Modules**: `app -> feature -> core:{ui,mvi,domain}`; `app -> core:data -> core:network ->
  core:api`. Features never depend on `core:data`, `core:network`, `core:api` or each other.
- **MVI**: each screen has immutable `State`, `Event` and one-shot `Effect` types, a
  `BaseViewModel`, a `Route` that wires Koin and a stateless, previewable `Screen`.
- **Design system**: use `Oc*` components and `OcTheme` tokens, no hard-coded colors
  ([`docs/design-system.md`](docs/design-system.md)). Every interactive control has a
  `testTag`.
- **Strings**: in resources, English in `values`. Keep all supported translations in sync
  (`es`, `fr`, `de`, `it`, `pt-BR`, `ru`, `zh-Hans`, `ja`, `ko`, `ar`), preserving format
  arguments and locale-specific plurals. Run `bun test tools/locales.test.ts` from the root.
- **Server contract**: `android/core/api` is generated from `api/openapi.json`; never edit it
  and never hand-write DTOs. Run `bun run generate` in `tools/api-gen` after changing
  the spec (Bun and Java are needed; `bun run refresh` pulls the spec from a local server).
- **Formatting**: ktlint through Spotless, configured in
  [`android/.editorconfig`](android/.editorconfig), which Android Studio also reads. Run
  `./gradlew spotlessApply` in `android/` to fix formatting before committing.
- **Tests**: ViewModels and repositories get unit tests next to their module; fixtures are
  shared in `core:testing` and contain only neutral data.

## Commits and pull request titles

Pull requests are squash-merged, so the **PR title becomes the commit on `main`** and the
release notes. Titles follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org) with
a capitalized subject:

```
type(scope): Subject starting with a capital letter
```

| Types | Use for |
|---|---|
| `feat` | A new feature |
| `fix` | A bug fix |
| `perf` | A performance improvement |
| `refactor` | Code changes that neither fix a bug nor add a feature |
| `docs` | Documentation only |
| `test` | Tests only |
| `build`, `ci` | Gradle, dependencies, scripts, workflows |
| `style`, `chore`, `revert` | Formatting, maintenance, reverts |

Optional scopes: `chat`, `sessions`, `connect`, `settings`, `ui`, `data`, `network`, `api`,
`deps`, `release`. Examples: `feat(chat): Group thinking and tool rows`,
`fix(connect): Validate the server URL`. Add `!` after the type for breaking changes.

## Pull requests

- Fill in the template: what changed, how you verified it, screenshots for UI changes
  (light and dark theme).
- Say which platforms you tested on. Most code is shared, so a change usually reaches both the
  Android and the iOS app; if you could only run one of them, tick "Only tested on one
  platform" too. The pull request then gets `needs:ios-check` or `needs:android-check`, and a
  maintainer ticks the other platform after trying it there, which removes the label.
- Keep each pull request to one change; no unrelated edits.
- CI must pass: formatting, unit tests, lint, debug build and the generated API check.
- [CodeRabbit](https://coderabbit.ai) reviews every pull request automatically. Its comments
  are suggestions: reply or resolve them, a maintainer makes the final call.

## Releases

Releases are automated with [release-please](https://github.com/googleapis/release-please):

1. After every merge to `main`, a pull request titled `chore(release): Release x.y.z` is
   opened or updated. It bumps `version.txt` and adds the new entries to `CHANGELOG.md`.
   `feat` bumps the minor version, `fix` and `perf` the patch version, and `!` the major
   version (minor while the version is below 1.0).
2. When a maintainer merges it, the release is tagged, published on GitHub Releases, and the
   signed APK, its R8 mapping file and SHA-256 checksums are attached.

Only `feat`, `fix`, `perf`, `revert` and `docs` appear in the changelog. The app's version
name and code come from `version.txt` (1.2.3 becomes version code 1002003).

# Security

## Reporting a vulnerability

Please report vulnerabilities privately through GitHub: open the **Security** tab of this
repository and choose **Report a vulnerability**. Do not open a public issue. You will get an
answer as soon as possible, and credit in the release notes if you want it.

## How the app handles your server

- The app talks to your own OpenCode server with HTTP Basic auth, using the server password
  or a token obtained by pairing (`opencode pair`).
- Credentials are stored encrypted on the device (Android Keystore) and are never logged.
- While the connect screen is open, the app looks for OpenCode on port 4096 of the local
  Wi-Fi or Ethernet subnet (at most 254 addresses). It only requests the public web manifest
  and never sends credentials during the scan.
- Transcripts are cached on the device so chats open quickly; uninstalling the app or removing
  the server deletes them.
- OpenCode servers usually run over **plain HTTP**, so the app allows cleartext traffic.
  Anyone on the same network path can read the traffic, including the credentials. Reach the
  server over a network you trust (home LAN or a VPN such as WireGuard or Tailscale), or put
  it behind HTTPS. **Never expose the OpenCode port directly to the internet.**

# OpenCode Mobile design system

The app mirrors the OpenCode V2 web UI: dense but calm, neutral greys, hairline borders,
small radii, accent used sparingly. Everything lives in `android/core/ui`
(`io.github.beppe2880.opencodemobile.core.ui`). Feature code uses only these tokens and `Oc*` components;
no hard-coded colors outside `theme/OcColors.kt`.

## Theme entry points

| API | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `OcTheme(darkTheme, openCodeTheme) { }` | Provides `LocalOcColors` and a Material 3 `ColorScheme`, typography and shapes mapped from the tokens. `openCodeTheme` is the id of an OpenCode theme (below); null keeps the app's own colors. |
| `ThemeMode.isDark()` | Resolves `AppSettings.theme` (System / Light / Dark): the requested mode. |
| `isDarkTheme(openCodeTheme, dark)` | Whether the app is actually dark: an OpenCode theme with a single mode keeps it. System bar icons follow this (inside `OcTheme`, `OcTheme.colors.isDark`). |
| `OcTheme.colors` | Full token set (`OcColors`), including state, agent and diff colors, and the markdown, syntax and terminal colors of an OpenCode theme. |
| `OcTheme.markdown` | The markdown colors of the active OpenCode theme, null without one. |
| `OcTheme.mono` | IBM Plex Mono styles: `code`, `codeSmall`, `label`. |
| `OcSpacing`, `OcRadius` | Spacing and corner scales. |

Material components keep working because the token set is mapped onto `MaterialTheme.colorScheme`
(`primary = bg-accent`, `surface = bg-base`, `background = bg-deep`, `outlineVariant = border-base`,
`error = danger.fg`, ...). Prefer `OcTheme.colors.*` in app code for anything beyond Material defaults.

## OpenCode themes

The user can give the whole app the colors of one of the OpenCode terminal app's (TUI) built-in
themes, like `/theme` there. `OpenCodeThemes.all` lists them ("opencode", the TUI default, first,
then alphabetical); `OpenCodeTheme` has the `light` and `dark` `OpenCodeThemeTokens` and a
`preview(dark)` swatch for the picker. No theme (null) keeps the colors above, unchanged.

The colors are generated, never hand-written: `tools/themes` resolves the TUI's theme files (cached
in `tools/themes/assets` at the pinned OpenCode tag) with OpenCode's own `@opencode/theme`
(`migrateV1` for V1 files, `parseThemeDocument`, `resolveThemeDocument` per mode) and writes
`core/ui/.../theme/generated/OpenCodeThemes.kt`. A theme with only one mode has it in both, so it
stays dark (or light) whatever the app mode: `OcColors.isDark`, the Material scheme and the system
bars follow the theme. CI fails when the file is stale (`bun run check` in `tools/themes`); to
update, `bun add @opencode/theme@<version>` (exact version), `bun run refresh`.

`OpenCodeThemeTokens.toOcColors()` (`theme/OpenCodeColors.kt`) maps a theme like the TUI uses it:

| `OcColors` | OpenCode token |
|---|---|
| `bgDeep`, `bgBase`, `textInverse` | `background.base` |
| `layer01`, `bgCodePath`, `userBubbleBg` | `background.raised.base` (panels; the TUI's user message) |
| `layer02`, `borderMuted` | `background.raised.high` (menus) |
| `layer03` | `background.raised.max` |
| `layer04` | halfway between `background.raised.max` and `text.muted` |
| `textBase`, `bgInverse`, `iconBase`, `userBubbleText` | `text.base` |

# Mobile browser provider authentication

Android supports OpenAI's **Sign in with ChatGPT** (`openai/chatgpt-token-sharing`).
This is not the legacy Codex device flow. Other browser methods remain disabled.
The shared engine has an explicit provider adapter; server discovery alone does not
supply client registration, endpoints, scopes, redirect policy or credential metadata.
iOS browser authentication is disabled pending a native loopback listener and verifier.

## Ownership and security

- The phone opens the system browser and listens only on `127.0.0.1`, at an ephemeral
  port with `/auth/callback`. PKCE S256, random state and nonce are per attempt.
- Invalid paths, duplicate parameters, mismatched state, unexpected Host, POSTs and
  cross-origin requests are rejected. Reads are bounded; an attempt expires after five minutes.
- The phone exchanges the code using the exact redirect and the callback's issued client ID.
  Required token-sharing scope and ID-token RS256 signature, issuer, audience,
  subject, nonce and validity are checked against OpenAI's HTTPS JWKS.
- OAuth requests use an isolated, unauthenticated HTTP client with redirects disabled.
  Credentials are imported through the generated `/api/credential` client, with
  authenticated TLS and redirects disabled. Literal local loopback is also permitted
  for local development (for example `adb reverse`); LAN/VPN HTTP is not presumed protected.
- The import contains method ID, access/refresh token, expiry, issued client ID and scopes.
  It neither reads all server credentials nor modifies the server plugin's host-ID store.
  The phone's stable **local authorizing host ID** is separate; it is never imported.
  Before local authorization, an unopened server OAuth attempt is prepared and immediately
  cancelled: the existing plugin initializes/preserves its own host ID before import.
- Tokens and codes are temporary in-memory values, never saved to settings, drafts,
  logs or clipboard; tokens are never put in URLs. Closing the panel, changing server or cancelling its scope
  releases the listener. Process death requires starting again. Only the server refreshes tokens.
- A cancelled import may already have reached the server; no automatic delete or
  refresh/retry is attempted. Model caches are invalidated before and after connection.
- After checking state and callback parameters, the phone returns HTTP 202 with a neutral
  receipt: return to the app to complete sign-in. This is not a success/verification page.
  The listener is released immediately; the code remains only in the owning coroutine.
- Token exchange, JWKS retrieval and credential import wait for app visibility. Android
  can block networking for a background UID while still delivering the loopback callback;
  this can surface as a DNS failure even with correct DNS settings. No foreground service,
  DNS override or change to VPN settings is needed. Foreground waits are bounded to five
  minutes and closing the panel cancels them; the local authorization also has its existing
  five-minute deadline. Only the app confirms verification and server import.
  OAuth/server error bodies are never displayed.

## Verification limits

Tests use generated RSA keys and fake provider responses for successful authorization
and credential import; actual sockets test callback handling and cancellation.
Live emulator checks do not sign into personal accounts. Completing consent, using a
real ChatGPT-plan token, and subsequent server refresh require user-assisted verification.

Failures include a safe diagnostic such as `OAUTH_TokenExchange_HTTP_400` or
`OAUTH_Claims`. Stages distinguish server preparation, callback, token exchange,
scope, response shape, JWKS download, signature, claims, target-server changes,
credential import and expiry. Only fixed identifiers and an available HTTP status
reach the UI; original exception messages, response bodies and causes are discarded.
Native transport failures additionally include an allowlisted category (DNS, connection,
certificate, TLS, socket timeout, interrupted I/O, connection I/O, protocol or other I/O)
and elapsed milliseconds from a monotonic clock, for example
`OAUTH_TokenExchange_DNS_42ms`. An interrupted I/O operation is not assumed to be a
timeout just from its message. Response-body transport failures retain HTTP status when
available. No hostnames, messages or stack traces are copied into diagnostics. OAuth
POST connection retries remain disabled: a lost response must not silently reuse a code.
An import error cannot prove the server did not save: check provider status before retrying.
An absent `expires_in` defaults to one hour, matching the server plugin. Explicit
malformed, non-positive or overflowing expiry values still fail validation; a valid
expiry is not artificially restricted to one day. All OIDC checks remain required.

# Running The Benchmarks

All commands run from `android/`. Pick the device with `ANDROID_SERIAL` (discover it with
`adb devices -l`; never hard-code a serial in scripts or docs).

## Run

```bash
# Free the device from other UiAutomator clients.
adb -s <serial> shell pkill -f mobilecli

# Everything (about ten minutes on an emulator).
ANDROID_SERIAL=<serial> ./gradlew :benchmark:connectedBenchmarkAndroidTest

# One class while iterating.
ANDROID_SERIAL=<serial> ./gradlew :benchmark:connectedBenchmarkAndroidTest \
  -Pandroid.testInstrumentationRunnerArguments.class=io.github.beppe2880.opencodemobile.benchmarks.IdleWorkBenchmark
```

The task builds and installs `app-benchmark.apk` (`io.github.beppe2880.opencodemobile.benchmark`)
and the test APK (`io.github.beppe2880.opencodemobile.benchmarks`), and removes them
afterwards. The installed release and debug apps are not touched.

## Read The Results

Results are JSON, one file per run, with the Perfetto traces beside it:

```text
benchmark/build/outputs/connected_android_test_additional_output/benchmark/connected/<device>/
```

```bash
f=$(find benchmark/build/outputs -name '*benchmarkData.json' | head -1)
jq -r '.benchmarks[] | "\(.className | split(".") | last).\(.name): " + ((
  [.metrics | to_entries[] | "\(.key) median=\(.value.median) min=\(.value.minimum) max=\(.value.maximum)"] +
  [(.sampledMetrics // {}) | to_entries[] | "\(.key) P50=\(.value.P50) P90=\(.value.P90) P99=\(.value.P99)"]
) | join(" | "))' "$f"
```

`metrics` holds one value per iteration (counts, startup time); `sampledMetrics` holds the
per-frame samples of `FrameTimingMetric` as percentiles (`frameDurationCpuMs`,
`frameOverrunMs`; a positive overrun is a missed frame).

A failed test is in `benchmark/build/outputs/androidTest-results/connected/benchmark/*.xml`
and the HTML report under `benchmark/build/reports/androidTests/`. "Not on screen after
10000ms" means the demo did not reach the expected screen: check the selector in
`Demo.kt` against the app's test tags.

To keep a baseline, copy the JSON out of `build/` before the next run (the directory is
replaced), run again on the changed code, and compare medians.

## What The Idle Numbers Mean

`IdleWorkBenchmark` leaves each screen alone for 10 s after a 3 s settle:

| Test | Screen | Expect |
|---|---|---|
| `chatOfIdleSession` | a chat with nothing at work | about 0 frames, a few ms of CPU: the reference |
| `sessionListWithRunningSessions` | demo list, sessions at work | close to the reference |
| `chatWithRunningAgent` | chat of a working session | close to the reference |

A running screen near 600 frames means something on it animates every frame.

## Add A Test

1. Add or reuse a selector in `Demo.kt`; tags come from the app's `testTag`s.
2. Add a `@Test` to the class that owns the metric (`IdleWorkBenchmark` for a still

3. Navigate in `setupBlock` after `restartDemo()`; measure only the block.

# Koin Module Verification

Koin's JVM `Module.verify()` API can catch missing constructor definitions
without starting Android or creating every object. Verify the same composition
the application starts:

```text
dataModule + appModule
```

Do not verify each module only in isolation; cross-module bindings are the main
risk.

Declare runtime-provided types explicitly:

- Android `Context`/`Application`.
- ViewModel injected parameters (for example the chat session ID) through
  verification's injected-parameter declarations.

Keep a runtime smoke check too: verification cannot prove encrypted storage
initialization, camera availability or route-specific parameter values.

# Generator Pipeline

`tools/api-gen/src/generate.ts` (`bun run generate`) runs these steps in a temporary directory:

1. `tools/api-gen/src/augment-events.ts`
   - Converts `EventManifest.ServerDefinitions` + `ServerEvent.Connected` from
     `@opencode/schema` (Effect Schema) to JSON Schema with
     `Schema.toJsonSchemaDocument`.
   - Adds the definitions to `components.schemas`, renaming wire-named events
     (`session.text.delta`) to `SessionTextDeltaEvent`, and adds `OpenCodeEvent`.
   - Types the `/api/event` stream with `OpenCodeEvent`.
   - Patches known server/schema mismatches (`server.connected` has no `created`).
   - Deduplicates repeated tags (generator validation fails otherwise).
2. `tools/api-gen/src/prepare-spec.ts`
   - Keeps only `GET /api/config` of the `config` area and narrows its response to
     `{ type, info: { model } }` (`ConfigModelEntry`), since the app reads only the global
     model; the full config schema would add dozens of classes and change shared models.
     `model` (string or object) is raw JSON, mapped in `ResourceMapping.configuredModel()`.
   - `anyOf` unions whose members share a constant (`type`, `status`, `_tag`,
     `kind`) become `oneOf` + `discriminator`, so the generator emits sealed
     interfaces instead of one flattened class with every field required.
   - Removes `additionalProperties: true` from structs (Effect default) so models
     are data classes, not `HashMap` subclasses.
   - Mixed primitive unions (`number | false`) become free-form JSON; the Kotlin
     generator cannot serialize them. Unions mixing primitives and primitive arrays
     count too, and already converted nested unions are marked `x-raw-json`, because
     the walk is post-order: without that, `Form.Value` silently lost `number`.
     Form answers are therefore `JsonElement` (mapped in `FormMapping.kt`).
   - Flattens deepObject query objects to `location[directory]` scalars.
   - Keeps only `KEEP_TAGS` operations and reachable schemas.
3. openapi-generator flags that matter:
   - Two runs with the same spec and flags. Models come from `library=jvm-retrofit2` +
     `generateOneOfAnyOfWrappers=true`: only this combination generates sealed kotlinx
     union serializers (the `multiplatform` library flattens unions into
     `actualInstance: Any?` and duplicates `@Serializable`). APIs, `auth/` and
     `infrastructure/` come from `library=multiplatform` (Ktor). Model names match, so the
     two halves compile together in `commonMain`.
   - `@JvmInline` gets an explicit `kotlin.jvm.JvmInline` import: jvm-retrofit2 relies on
     the implicit JVM import, which common code lacks.
   - `dateLibrary=string`: the multiplatform library rejects java.time.
   - `enumPropertyNaming=UPPERCASE`: an enum constant named `context` breaks
     Kotlin 2.2 parsing (context parameters).
   - Type mappings: `integer=Long` (millisecond timestamps), `number=Double`,
     free-form `object=JsonObject`, `AnyType=JsonElement`.

Validated against OpenCode 2.0.27: every message type and 317/318 recorded events
decode; the remaining one was fixed by the `server.connected` patch.

When upgrading the generator, regenerate, compile `:core:api`, then run the
fixture tests in `core:network`.

# Compose Performance Diagnosis

Use one reproducible interaction and one primary hypothesis.

1. Confirm that visible data did not legitimately change.
2. Capture recomposition counts or Compose compiler reports for the shipped
   variant.
3. Classify the issue:
   - stable versus unstable parameter comparison;
   - new unstable instances created by the caller;
   - fast-changing State read in composition instead of layout/draw;
   - snapshot state written back across phases;
   - expensive work performed during composition;
   - lazy item identity/key problem.
4. Apply the smallest truthful fix.
5. Repeat the same measurement.

With Kotlin 2.2 strong skipping, unstable parameters do not automatically make a
restartable composable non-skippable. Inspect comparison semantics and instance
churn before adding annotations or memoization.

Do not call fewer recompositions an improvement when frame time, allocations,
or user-visible latency did not improve.

# Perfetto Workflow

Use Perfetto/System Trace for startup, frame jank, CPU scheduling, blocking IO,
binder, memory pressure, and service interactions that source inspection cannot
quantify.

1. Use a release-like/profileable build on a representative device or emulator.
2. Define one scenario and start/end marker before capture.
3. Enable only data sources needed for the hypothesis to keep the trace useful.
4. Reproduce once without unrelated interaction.
5. Inspect the main thread, RenderThread, binder, coroutine/worker threads,
   frame timeline, and IO around the marker.
6. Use Trace Processor SQL for repeated slices, long main-thread work, frame
   misses, or startup phases when visual inspection is insufficient.
7. Record baseline and after measurements from the same scenario/build/device.

Macrobenchmark lives in `android/benchmark` (see the `android-benchmarks` skill); its runs
save a Perfetto trace per iteration next to the results. No Baseline Profile module is
configured; introducing one is a dedicated performance task.

# iOS Simulator Automation

The simulator has no ADB. UI automation uses the DeviceKit XCUITest runner
(`com.mobilenext.devicekit-iosUITests.xctrunner`, installed by Mobile MCP), which
serves JSON-RPC on `127.0.0.1:12004` of the Mac.

## Start

```bash
xcrun simctl boot <udid>            # skip when already booted
open -a Simulator
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:12004/health || \
  xcrun simctl launch booted com.mobilenext.devicekit-iosUITests.xctrunner
```

Poll `/health` with a deadline before sending commands.

## Commands

`scripts/ios.py` (copy it to the Mac) wraps the RPC calls:

```bash
python3 ios.py ui                 # accessibility tree: type, label, value, center (points)
python3 ios.py tap "Settings"     # tap by exact label, then by substring
python3 ios.py tapxy 196 440      # tap at points (393x852 on iPhone 15)
python3 ios.py longpress "label"
python3 ios.py text "hello"       # type into the focused field
python3 ios.py swipe 196 700 196 250
python3 ios.py key home
python3 ios.py shot name          # /tmp/name.png, scaled to 1000 px high
```

Raw call: `curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:12004/rpc -d
'{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"device.io.tap","params":{"x":196,"y":478,"deviceId":"any"},"id":1}'`.
Other methods: `device.dump.ui`, `device.io.text`, `device.io.swipe`,
`device.clipboard.set`, `device.apps.launch` / `terminate` (`{"bundleId": ...}`).

## Pitfalls

- Coordinates are points, not screenshot pixels: divide screenshot pixels by the
  scale (`device.info`).
- `testTag`s are not exposed; target controls by accessibility label. Controls
  without one (e.g. a FAB with only an icon and text in a custom layout) may be
  missing from the tree: tap by coordinates and report the accessibility gap.
- `device.clipboard.set` briefly brings DeviceKit to the foreground; wait about
  3 s before tapping in the app, or the tap is lost in the transition.
- Typing a full pairing link character by character into the server URL field
  triggers the app's link detection midway. Type the base URL, move to the code
  field (keyboard "next"), then type the code; or paste the link.
- Launching the runner sends the app to the background; relaunch it with
  `device.apps.launch`.
- A freshly written screenshot may need a moment before another tool can read it.

# Build the Right Artifact for the Feedback Loop

A release binary takes roughly an order of magnitude longer to build than a
debug binary, and umbrella tasks such as `build` and `assemble` compile the
same code several times. Map each feedback loop to one specific task.

## Task table

| Feedback loop | Correct task |
|---|---|
| Xcode builds and runs the app (direct integration) | `:shared:embedAndSignAppleFrameworkForXcode` |
| Gradle-only check of the Apple Silicon simulator framework | `:shared:linkDebugFrameworkIosSimulatorArm64` |
| CocoaPods integration | `:shared:linkPodDebugFrameworkIosSimulatorArm64` |
| Distribution or App Store validation | `assemble<Name>ReleaseXCFramework` — in CI, not in the local loop |
| Debug XCFramework genuinely required | `assemble<Name>DebugXCFramework` |

Per-target link tasks follow the pattern
`link<BuildType>Framework<Target>`; find the exact names with
`./gradlew :shared:tasks` or in the build log.

## Rules

- `embedAndSignAppleFrameworkForXcode` builds only the slice Xcode asked for
  and must run from an Xcode build phase, not standalone. Direct integration
  uses the documented run-script phase; keep its
  `OVERRIDE_KOTLIN_BUILD_IDE_SUPPORTED` guard so the IDE does not trigger a
  second Gradle invocation.
- Do not mix integration methods: a project either uses direct integration or
  the CocoaPods integration, and the local task must match the one in use.
- Do not replace CI release artifacts with debug artifacts. If CI release
  builds are slow, fix caching, the target matrix, and exports instead.

## Target matrix

`*XCFramework` tasks build every declared target. Remove a target only when
project policy confirms it is unused — the common case is dropping
`iosX64()` when the team no longer supports Intel-based simulators. State the
policy assumption in your report; if policy is unclear, ask instead of
deleting.

Docs:
https://kotlinlang.org/docs/multiplatform-ios-integration-overview.html,
https://kotlinlang.org/docs/multiplatform/multiplatform-direct-integration.html,
https://kotlinlang.org/docs/multiplatform/multiplatform-build-native-binaries.html

# Caching and Gradle Configuration

Safe for every scenario; apply these before anything else.

## Update Kotlin

The latest Kotlin version is the first official recommendation for
Kotlin/Native compilation time — each release improves compiler performance.
Check `gradle/libs.versions.toml` or the plugin block and propose an upgrade
if the project is behind. Read the compatibility guide for the target release
before upgrading; for example, use the
[Kotlin 2.4 compatibility guide](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/compatibility-guide-24.html)
when moving to Kotlin 2.4.x. Each target release has a corresponding
compatibility guide. See the
[Kotlin 2.3.20 release notes](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/whatsnew2320.html#new-dsl-for-disabling-compilation-cache)
for the related cache change.

## Remove stale workarounds

Projects accumulate workarounds for long-fixed compiler issues. Upgrade Kotlin
first, then inspect:

- `kotlin.native.disableCompilerDaemon=true`
- `org.gradle.daemon=false`

Each disables a performance feature. Remove stale workarounds and check
whether the build completes successfully.

## Enable Gradle caching

```properties
# gradle.properties
org.gradle.caching=true
org.gradle.configuration-cache=true
```

- Trial the configuration cache with the user's real task before committing
  it. If Gradle reports configuration-cache problems, fix the blockers listed
  in the HTML report instead of abandoning the cache.
- The configuration cache implicitly enables parallel task execution, which
  can run several `link*` tasks at once and overload the machine (KT-70915).
  If that happens, bound it with `org.gradle.workers.max` in
  `gradle.properties` or `--max-workers` on the command line — do not turn
  the cache off for this reason alone.
- Delete `org.gradle.configureondemand=true`. Kotlin Multiplatform does not
  support Configuration on Demand, and it is not the same feature as the
  configuration cache.
- For CI, a remote Gradle build cache extends `org.gradle.caching` across
  machines.

## Keep `~/.konan` warm in CI

Kotlin/Native stores its compiler distribution and caches in `$HOME/.konan`.
Ephemeral CI machines and containers that lose it pay the cold-start cost on
every build. On GitHub Actions:

```yaml
- uses: actions/cache@v4
  with:
    path: ~/.konan
    key: konan-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('**/libs.versions.toml') }}
```

Use the `konan.data.dir` Gradle property only when the project intentionally
relocates that directory (for example, to a cacheable path on a CI runner).

Docs: https://kotlinlang.org/docs/native-improving-compilation-time.html and
https://kotlinlang.org/docs/gradle-compilation-and-caches.html

# Experimental Switches

Offer these last, label them experimental in the report, and keep them out of
the default recommendation set. Get the user's agreement before enabling any
of them.

## Incremental compilation of klib artifacts

```properties
# gradle.properties
kotlin.incremental.native=true
```

Recompiles only the changed part of a klib into the final binary, which helps
warm rebuilds after small edits. If it causes broken or inconsistent builds,
revert it and file a YouTrack issue with a minimized reproducer.

## smallBinary

The `smallBinary` binary option sets `-Oz` as the default LLVM optimization
level to shrink release binaries and their link time. It can cost runtime
performance, so verify hot paths before keeping it. It applies to release
binaries — it is not a fix for slow debug loops.

## LLVM backend customization

Customizing the LLVM backend is a last resort when nothing else helps, and is
out of scope for a routine performance pass — point the user at the official
documentation instead of improvising compiler flags.

Docs: https://kotlinlang.org/docs/native-binary-options.html and
https://kotlinlang.org/docs/native-improving-compilation-time.html

# Framework Exports and Generated Code

## Framework exports

Every exported module grows the API surface the compiler and linker must
keep.

- Remove `transitiveExport = true`. It exports the entire transitive closure
  and disables dead code elimination in many cases — it is almost never what
  the project actually needs.
- Keep an explicit `export(...)` only for modules whose API Swift or
  Objective-C code calls directly.

```kotlin
// Before: exports everything analytics depends on, defeats DCE
binaries.framework {
    export(project(":analytics"))
    transitiveExport = true
}

// After: exports exactly the Swift-facing API
binaries.framework {
    export(project(":analytics"))
}
```

If Swift code stops compiling after narrowing exports, add back only the
specific modules it references — that is the export list the project really
needs.

## Generated code

If `ksp*` tasks dominate the measured time, report the bottleneck as
generated-code work — do not present a Kotlin/Native tweak as the fix.

- Scope KSP to the targets or source sets that need generated code instead of
  a broad `ksp(...)` dependency:

  ```kotlin
  dependencies {
      add("kspCommonMainMetadata", libs.myprocessor)
      add("kspIosSimulatorArm64", libs.myprocessor)
  }
  ```

- Confirm the generated sources are consumed by the corresponding native
  compilation before adding another target-specific KSP configuration.

Docs: https://kotlinlang.org/docs/ksp-multiplatform.html and
https://kotlinlang.org/docs/native-improving-compilation-time.html

# Evidence And Metrics

## Evidence Labels

Use the strongest label actually earned:

- `Observed (rendered)`: visible in the running product.
- `Observed (interaction)`: happened while exercising the flow.
- `Observed (code)`: present in source; rendering remains unverified.
- `Measured`: directly timed or counted during a repeatable run.
- `Computed`: derived from stated inputs and a documented rubric.
- `Inferred`: strongly implied by available evidence but not observed.
- `Predicted preference`: a persona-based AI judgment, not user research.
- `Hypothesis`: plausible and unverified.
- `Analytics required`: behavior or preference cannot be settled without data.
- `User research required`: a real-user preference or mental model must be
  tested rather than predicted.

Never write "users prefer" from a predicted preference. Write which simulated
perspective would likely prefer an option, why, and with what confidence.

## Flow Metrics

Count only what the defined task actually requires:

- screens or materially distinct states;
- click/tap/keyboard actions;
- decisions the user must make;
- manual fields or values;
- navigation depth and context switches;
- waits and waits without feedback;
- scroll needed to reach required actions;
- backtracking;
- error opportunities and recovery actions;
- time to value, only when measured or explicitly marked estimated.

Do not optimize click count in isolation. Three obvious actions can cost less
than one ambiguous action.

## Interaction Cost Rubric

Use this only to compare alternatives for the same goal. It is not a scientific
UX score and must not be compared across unrelated products.

| Event | Cost |
|---|---:|
| Obvious action with immediate feedback | 1 |
| Obvious navigation step | 1 |
| Simple decision with clear consequences | 2 |
| Necessary manual input | 2 |
| Input the system could already know | 3 |
| Context switch or hidden-menu navigation | 3 |
| Ambiguous decision | 4 |
| Wait without useful feedback | 4 |
| Backtracking | 5 |
| Error recovery | 5 |

Record irreversible or high-stakes risk separately; never trade safety for a
lower score. State each counted event so another reviewer can reproduce the
total. Avoid percentages unless both baseline and result were measured with the
same method.

## Confidence

- `High`: direct runtime evidence supports the conclusion.
- `Medium`: evidence is partial or the conclusion includes a prediction.
- `Low`: description-only or major states were unavailable.

Split confidence when needed: high confidence in measured cost can coexist with
medium confidence in predicted preference.
